definition:
A prophet in the Bible is a person who speaks for God. The prophets addressed their own day first: they called Israel back to the covenant, confronted kings, defended the poor, warned of judgment, and comforted the broken. They also spoke of what God would yet do, and the New Testament reads Jesus as the one in whom those promises come true. Students often put it this way: biblical prophecy is more ‘forthtelling’ than ‘foretelling’, speaking God's word into the present, though it includes genuine prediction. Fulfillment in the Bible is broader than prediction coming true. Sometimes a prophet names an event before it happens; more often a pattern God set in Israel's history, a king, a sacrifice, an exodus, a temple, is filled out and completed in Christ. How much biblical prophecy still awaits fulfillment is a question on which Christians differ.

The usual Hebrew word for prophet is nabi', probably ‘one who is called’ or ‘one who announces’, though its origin is uncertain and its meaning is best learned from how it is used. Older names were ro'eh and chozeh, both meaning ‘seer’ (1 Samuel 9:9). Prophetic speech is marked by formulas such as ‘thus says the LORD’ and ne'um YHWH, ‘the declaration of the LORD’, which the BSB renders ‘declares the LORD’. An oracle is often called a massa', traditionally ‘burden’, though many scholars now take it simply as ‘pronouncement’. In Greek the prophet is prophētēs and prophecy is prophēteia. The New Testament's key verb for fulfillment is plēroō, ‘to fill’ or ‘to complete’, and its word for a pattern that points ahead is typos, ‘type’ or ‘example’ (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11).
ot:
The first promise of a coming deliverer is often found in Genesis 3:15, where God tells the serpent that the woman's seed “will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” Many Christians since Irenaeus have read it as the first announcement of the gospel; others read it first as a statement of lasting hostility between humans and evil, which the New Testament later sees resolved in Christ. Abraham is the first person called a prophet (Genesis 20:7), and there the word describes one who intercedes, not one who predicts. Jacob's blessing promises that the scepter will not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and Balaam, a foreign seer, sees a star and a scepter rising from Israel (Numbers 24:17). Moses is the model prophet. God speaks with him “face to face, clearly and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:8), and Moses longs for the day when all the LORD's people would be prophets (Numbers 11:29). Deuteronomy promises a prophet like Moses into whose mouth God will put his words (Deuteronomy 18:15-18), and it gives Israel two tests. A prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken from the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:22), and a prophet who works signs but leads the people after other gods must not be heeded even if the sign comes to pass (Deuteronomy 13:1-3). Fidelity to the covenant God matters more than wonders.

In the historical books prophets stand beside kings. Samuel was confirmed as a prophet because the LORD let none of his words fall to the ground (1 Samuel 3:19-20). Nathan brought God's promise to David that his offspring would reign forever (2 Samuel 7:12-16), the promise on which later messianic hope rests, and then confronted David over Bathsheba. Elijah and Elisha fought the worship of Baal in the ninth century BC, and Micaiah, surrounded by four hundred court prophets telling King Ahab what he wanted to hear, said he would speak only what the LORD told him (1 Kings 22:14). From the eighth century the prophets' words were gathered into books. Amos, a herdsman from Judah sent to the northern kingdom around 760 BC, insisted he was no professional prophet (Amos 7:14-15). Hosea, Isaiah, and Micah warned of Assyria, which destroyed Samaria in 722 BC. Jeremiah and Ezekiel spoke through Babylon's conquest of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Their message was mostly about the present: idolatry, injustice, and false security. Micah's summary is typical, to act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly with God (Micah 6:8).

The prophets also looked ahead, and they did so in ways that show how prophecy works. Many warnings were conditional. God says through Jeremiah that if a nation he has threatened turns from its evil, he will relent (Jeremiah 18:7-10), and when Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, God relented from the disaster he had threatened (Jonah 3:10). A prophecy's purpose was often to change its hearers, not merely to inform them. Other promises reached past the prophet's horizon: a son of David whose government will have no end (Isaiah 9:6-7), a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34), a Servant “pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5), a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), a king coming humble and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), a Spirit poured out on all people (Joel 2:28-29), and Elijah sent before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5). In Isaiah 40 to 48 God's ability to announce things before they happen is his argument against idols: “I declare the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:10). The prophets also knew false prophecy. Jeremiah condemned prophets who spoke “visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:16) and faced Hananiah, who promised peace that did not come (Jeremiah 28). Daniel stands somewhat apart: its visions of empires and of one like a son of man given everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13-14) belong to the kind of writing scholars call apocalyptic. Its date is contested. The traditional view places Daniel in the sixth century BC; most critical scholars date the visions to around 165 BC, in the crisis under Antiochus IV. Isaiah's authorship is similarly debated, many scholars assigning chapters 40 to 66 to later prophets of the exile and return, while others defend a single eighth-century author.
nt:
The New Testament opens by announcing fulfillment. Matthew uses the formula ‘this took place to fulfill’ again and again, and his uses show the range of the idea. Isaiah's sign of a child named Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14) is applied to the virgin birth (Matthew 1:22-23). The Hebrew word 'almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, rendered it parthenos, ‘virgin’. Many Christians read Isaiah as a direct prediction; others read it as a sign fulfilled first in Ahaz's own day and filled out more completely in Jesus; both readings affirm that Matthew teaches the virgin birth. When Matthew cites “Out of Egypt I called My Son” (Matthew 2:15), he quotes Hosea 11:1, which in context looks back on the exodus. Matthew is not claiming Hosea predicted the event; he is showing that Jesus relives Israel's story as the true Son, which is fulfillment by pattern rather than by forecast. Jesus himself read Isaiah 61 in the synagogue at Nazareth and said, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21), and he told his disciples that John the Baptist was the Elijah who was to come (Matthew 11:14).

After the resurrection Jesus taught that the whole Old Testament pointed to him. He rebuked the two disciples on the Emmaus road for being slow to believe “all that the prophets have spoken” and explained, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, what the Scriptures said about himself (Luke 24:25-27). The apostles preached the same way. At Pentecost Peter said, “this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16), and he identified Jesus as the prophet like Moses (Acts 3:22). Paul opened Romans with “the gospel He promised beforehand through His prophets in the Holy Scriptures” (Romans 1:2) and wrote that however many God's promises are, in Christ they are ‘Yes’ (2 Corinthians 1:20). Peter says the prophets themselves searched to learn the time and setting the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing to when he “predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow” (1 Peter 1:11), and that they were serving later readers, not only themselves. Hebrews reads the tabernacle and the sacrifices as “a copy and shadow” of heavenly realities (Hebrews 8:5, 10:1). The New Testament's way of reading the Old is therefore not a list of isolated proof texts but the conviction that Israel's whole story, its promises, institutions, and longings, finds its meaning in Jesus.

Prophecy did not end with the Old Testament. Joel's promise that sons and daughters would prophesy came true at Pentecost, and the church had prophets: Agabus predicted a famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28), Philip's four daughters prophesied (Acts 21:9), and Paul urged the Corinthians to desire the gift, which speaks “for their edification, encouragement, and comfort” (1 Corinthians 14:3). Such prophecy was to be weighed: “the others should weigh carefully what is said” (1 Corinthians 14:29), and the Thessalonians were told, “Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things” (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21). The church is built on “the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians 2:20). Whether this gift continues today, and in what form, is debated between continuationists and cessationists; the study of spiritual gifts treats it.

The New Testament also contains its own predictions: Jesus' discourse on the destruction of the temple and his coming (Matthew 24, Mark 13, Luke 21), Paul's teaching on the resurrection and the Lord's return, and the book of Revelation, which calls itself “the words of this prophecy” (Revelation 1:3). Jesus warned that “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36), and Peter answered scoffers who asked where the promise of his coming was by saying that the Lord is patient, “not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). The angel's word to John gathers the whole subject into one line: “the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy” (Revelation 19:10).

keyTexts.why: The promise that the woman's seed will crush the serpent's head. Many Christians read it as the first announcement of the gospel; all read it as the start of the long conflict Scripture resolves in Christ.
The promise of a prophet like Moses and the test of true prophecy. Acts 3:22 applies the promise to Jesus.
Nathan's promise that David's house and throne will endure forever. The root of the hope for a messianic son of David.
The sign of Immanuel, applied by Matthew to the virgin birth. A central text for how prediction and fulfillment relate.
God declares the end from the beginning. Prophecy is grounded in God's rule over history and set against the silence of idols.
The suffering Servant who bears the sins of many. The New Testament's most important prophetic text for the cross.
God's warnings and promises to nations can be conditional on their response. Prophecy often aims to change its hearers.
The promise of a new covenant written on the heart, quoted at length in Hebrews 8 as fulfilled in Christ.
One like a son of man receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus' favorite way of speaking of himself draws on this vision.
A look back at the exodus that Matthew reads as fulfilled in Jesus. Fulfillment by pattern rather than prediction.
The risen Jesus explains how Moses and all the Prophets spoke of him. The key to the New Testament's reading of the Old.
Peter reads Pentecost as the fulfillment of Joel's promise that God would pour out his Spirit on all people.
Prophecy in the church builds up, encourages, and comforts, and it is to be weighed by others.
The prophets searched for the time and setting of what the Spirit of Christ foretold, knowing they served later generations.
The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy. All true prophecy bears witness to him.

history:
The early church argued from prophecy more than from almost anything else. Justin Martyr, in his First Apology (around 155) and Dialogue with Trypho (around 160), set out at length how the Hebrew prophets had spoken of Christ's birth, suffering, and reign. The Didache, a church manual usually dated to the late first or early second century, told congregations how to test traveling prophets and gave practical signs of a false one, such as staying too long or asking for money. In the second half of the second century the movement called the New Prophecy, led by Montanus with the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla in Phrygia, claimed ecstatic revelations that extended the apostolic teaching; Tertullian later joined it, and the wider church rejected it. The experience helped fix the conviction that later prophecy is tested by the apostolic witness and does not add to it.

The church also argued about how to read prophecy. Origen of Alexandria (died around 253) sought spiritual senses beneath the letter; the school of Antioch, including Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia, insisted on the historical sense and read fewer Old Testament passages as direct predictions. Augustine, in the City of God (completed around 426), read the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the present age of the church, a reading that shaped Western theology for a millennium. The pagan philosopher Porphyry in the third century argued that Daniel was written in the time of Antiochus IV; we know his argument largely through Jerome's commentary on Daniel, which answered it. In the twelfth century Joachim of Fiore divided history into three ages and gave medieval prophecy speculation a lasting pattern. At the Reformation many Protestants read Revelation as a map of church history and identified the papacy with the Antichrist, a view written into the Westminster Confession (1646). Catholic scholars answered with other schemes: the Jesuit Francisco Ribera placed most of Revelation in the future, and Luis de Alcázar placed most of it in the first centuries.

The modern period added new pressures. In 1724 the deist Anthony Collins attacked the argument from prophecy, arguing that the New Testament's uses of the Old were not literal fulfillments. Critical scholarship dated books such as Daniel and parts of Isaiah later than tradition did, and some scholars concluded that apparent predictions were written after the events. Evangelical and Catholic scholars answered in different ways, some defending traditional dates and others arguing that fulfillment by pattern does not depend on the date of prediction; the Catholic scholar Raymond Brown wrote his dissertation (1955) on the idea of a ‘fuller sense’ intended by God beyond what the human author saw. John Nelson Darby (1800 to 1882) developed dispensationalism, which the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) spread widely, while George Eldon Ladd defended historic premillennialism and Reformed and Catholic theologians largely held the amillennial reading. William Miller's prediction that Christ would return by 1844 ended in what his followers called the Great Disappointment of October 22, 1844, a lasting warning against date setting.

differ.body: Many prophecies to Israel, including the land, the throne of David, and a restored nation, will be fulfilled literally to ethnic Israel in the future, and God's program for Israel remains distinct from his program for the church. Most of Revelation from chapter 4 on describes events still ahead: a future tribulation, the return of Christ, and a thousand-year reign on earth. Classic dispensationalists expect the church to be taken up before the tribulation. Defenders argue that God's promises must mean what they meant to their first hearers, that Romans 11:25-29 keeps a future for Israel, and that consistent literal reading protects prophecy from being spiritualized away.

Christ will return before a thousand-year reign on earth, as a natural reading of Revelation 20 suggests, but the church and Israel are one people of God in Christ, and the church will pass through the final tribulation. This view, held by many early Christian writers such as Irenaeus and in the twentieth century by George Eldon Ladd, reads much Old Testament prophecy as fulfilled in Christ and the church while still expecting a future earthly reign. Defenders argue that it takes both the New Testament's reading of the Old and the sequence of Revelation 19 and 20 seriously.

The promises to Israel find their fulfillment in Christ and in the people united to him, Jew and Gentile, and the thousand years of Revelation 20 is a symbol of the present age, in which Christ reigns and Satan is bound from deceiving the nations. The last things still ahead are one great event: Christ's return, the resurrection of all, the final judgment, and the new creation. Defenders, from Augustine to much of Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox teaching, argue that 2 Corinthians 1:20 and the New Testament's own readings of the prophets set the pattern, and that Revelation is symbolic literature to be read as such.

Much of what Jesus said in the Olivet Discourse and much of Revelation was fulfilled in the first century, above all in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in AD 70, since Jesus said this generation would not pass away until these things took place (Matthew 24:34). Christ's future bodily return, the resurrection, and the judgment are still to come. Many who hold this view are postmillennial, expecting the gospel to spread and prevail in the world before Christ returns. Defenders argue that it honors the time indicators in the texts, such as soon and near, and the confidence of the Great Commission.

errors:
The church has rejected the idea that prophecy is fortune-telling, a set of puzzles whose purpose is to satisfy curiosity about the future. Biblical prophecy calls people to repentance, faith, and faithfulness now; reading it chiefly to decode headlines turns it into the kind of divination the Law forbids. Date setting has been repeatedly discredited, from medieval predictions to the Millerite disappointment of 1844 and many since, and it contradicts Jesus' plain word that no one knows the day or the hour. The church has also rejected full preterism, the view that every prophecy, including Christ's return and the resurrection of the dead, was fulfilled by AD 70, because it denies what the creeds confess: that he will come again to judge the living and the dead.

On the other side stand the rejection of the Old Testament, as in Marcion, which cuts the gospel off from the promises it fulfills, and the assumption that prediction is impossible, which decides the question before examining the texts. The church has also rejected new prophecy that claims authority equal to or above the apostolic Scriptures, whether in the second century or later, because the apostles and prophets are the foundation and later words are tested by them. Finally, the New Testament's pattern of fulfillment warns against using prophecy to boost any nation or movement: the promises find their yes in Christ, not in a political program.
life:
The prophets were not first of all predictors; they were people who told the truth about God to people who did not want to hear it. Reading them well means letting them speak to us before we apply them to others, and hearing their demand for justice, mercy, and humility as addressed to the church as well as to the nations. The doctrine also gives a way to read the Old Testament: not as a collection of scattered predictions, but as a story whose promises and patterns come together in Jesus. A reader who sees that will find Christ in the Bible in ways that are honest to the text.

Fulfilled prophecy is also a ground of hope. The God who kept his promises to David, to the exiles, and in the coming of his Son can be trusted with the promises still outstanding: the return of Christ, the resurrection, and the renewal of all things. Christians who differ on the order of end-time events share that hope, and it steadies a life. It frees believers from both panic and complacency. They do not need to calculate dates, and they cannot treat the promise as irrelevant. They wait, as Peter says, knowing the Lord's patience means salvation.
questions: Matthew reads Hosea 11:1, which looks back on the exodus, as fulfilled in Jesus. What does that show about what fulfillment means in the Bible?
Jeremiah 18 and Jonah 3 show that some prophetic warnings depended on how people responded. How should that shape the way we read prophecies of judgment?
Christians differ on the order of events at the end, but share the hope of Christ's return. What would it look like to hold both the difference and the shared hope with integrity?
